responses.markdown:
## Summary of action
Start an 8–12 week sleep plan: limit time in bed to ~6 hours with a fixed wake time, use a 30–45 minute calming pre‑bed routine, avoid caffeine after 14:00 and alcohol within 4 hours of bed, raise the bed head 10–15 cm and avoid late meals, and add moderate aerobic activity 3×/week while aiming for gradual weight loss.

## What your sleep points to
Your overnight study shows short sleep (TST 269.5 minutes), low sleep efficiency (SE 55.9%), essentially no REM (REM 0.0%), mild sleep apnea (AHI 14.7 events/hour) and normal desaturations (ODI 0.4 events/hour). Future risks worth watching and acting on are: **Insomnia**, **Sleep disorders**, **Essential hypertension**, **Obesity**, **Anxiety disorder**, **Hyperlipidemia**.

## How the plan addresses these
Keeping a fixed wake time and reducing time in bed to about 6 hours will increase sleep pressure and improve sleep efficiency and REM over weeks; a 30–45 minute screen‑free wind‑down (relaxing reading, warm wash, slow breathing) helps settle anxiety at night. Stop caffeine after 14:00 and avoid alcohol within 4 hours of bed to reduce awakenings and REM suppression. To reduce reflux‑related arousals do not eat within ~3 hours of bed and raise the head of the bed 10–15 cm. Add moderate aerobic exercise (e.g., brisk walking 30–40 minutes, 3× weekly) and aim for slow weight loss (~0.5–1 kg/week) to help sleep quality and mild apnea; experimental data link sleep restriction to higher energy intake and visceral weight gain, so improving sleep and exercise helps both sleep and weight [2]. Chronic short sleep harms daytime thinking and function, so improving sleep matters for safety and cognition [1,4]. Nurse‑delivered sleep‑restriction/behavioral programs show real benefits for insomnia in trials [3]. If you have little improvement after 8–12 weeks or develop marked daytime sleepiness, contact your clinician to review next steps.

References
1. The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: dose-response effects on neurobehavioral functions and sleep physiology from chronic sleep restriction and total sleep deprivation — Sleep 2003. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12683469/
